danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 22
paragraphs: Vaklende i trængslen så Pierre sig om.
»Grev Pjotr Kirillovitj! Hvordan er De kommet herhen?« lød en stemme.

Pierre vendte sig om. Boris Drubetskoj (Julies mand), der børstede sine knæ med hånden (han havde nok tilsmudset dem, da han også havde knælet foran ikonet), kom hen til ham med et smil. Boris var elegant klædt med et let martialsk præg, passende for et felttog. Han bar en lang frakke og havde ligesom Kutuzov en ridepisk over skulderen.

Imens havde Kutuzov nået landsbyen og sat sig i skyggen af det nærmeste hus på en bænk, som en kosakker var løbet efter, og en anden hastigt havde dækket med et tæppe. Et vældigt og glimrende følge omgav ham.
Ikonet blev båret videre, ledsaget af mængden. Pierre standsede en snes skridt fra Kutuzov og talte med Boris.
Han forklarede sit ønske om at overvære slaget og se stillingen.

»Det må De gøre sådan her,« sagde Boris. »Jeg skal vise Dem lejren. De ser bedst alt fra det sted, hvor grev Bennigsen vil befinde sig. Jeg er tilknyttet ham, som De véd; jeg skal nævne det for ham. Men hvis De vil ride rundt om stillingen, så tag med os. Vi skal netop til venstre fløj. Når vi kommer tilbage, tilbring da natten hos mig, så arrangerer vi et spil kort. De kender naturligvis Dmitrij Sergejevitj? Det er hans kvarter,« og han pegede på det tredje hus i landsbyen Gorki.
»Men jeg ville gerne se højre fløj. Man siger, den er meget stærk,« sagde Pierre. »Jeg ville helst starte fra Moskva-floden og ride rundt om hele stillingen.«
»Det kan De gøre senere, men det vigtigste er venstre fløj.«
»Ja, ja. Men hvor er fyrst Bolkonskijs regiment? Kan De pege det ud for mig?«
»Fyrst Andrejs? Vi passerer det, og jeg fører Dem til ham.«
»Hvad med venstre fløj?« spurgte Pierre.

»Ærligt talt, mellem os, Gud alene véd, hvordan det står til med vores venstre fløj,« sagde Boris fortroligt og sænkede stemmen. »Det er slet ikke, som grev Bennigsen havde tænkt sig. Han ville befæste den bakke helt anderledes, men...« Boris trak på skuldrene. »Hans Durchlauchtighed ville det ikke, eller nogen overtalte ham. Ser De...« men Boris fik ikke talt færdigt, for i det øjeblik kom Kajsarov, Kutuzovs adjutant, hen til Pierre. »Nå, Kajsarov!« sagde Boris henvendt til ham med et ugenert smil. »Jeg prøvede netop at forklare greven vores stilling. Det er forbløffende, hvordan Hans Durchlauchtighed har kunnet forudse franskmændenes hensigter!«
»De mener venstre fløj?« spurgte Kajsarov.
»Ja, præcis; venstre fløj er nu overordentlig stærk.«

Selvom Kutuzov havde afskediget alle overflødige fra staben, havde Boris formået at forblive ved hovedkvarteret efter omorganiseringen. Han havde etableret sig hos grev Bennigsen, der ligesom alle, Boris havde tjent hos, anså den unge fyrst Drubetskoj for en uvurderlig mand.

I den øverste kommando var der to skarpt adskilte partier: Kutuzovs parti og Bennigsens, stabschefens. Boris tilhørte det sidste og kunne som ingen anden, samtidig med at han viste servil respekt for Kutuzov, skabe det indtryk, at den gamle ikke duede til meget, og at Bennigsen styrede alt. Nu var det afgørende øjeblik kommet, da Kutuzov enten ville gå til grunde, og magten overgå til Bennigsen, eller — selv om Kutuzov vandt — det ville fremstå som Bennigsens fortjeneste. Under alle omstændigheder ville der være mange store belønninger at uddele for morgendagens kamp, og nye mænd ville rykke frem. Så Boris var fuld af nervøs energi hele dagen.

Efter Kajsarov kom andre, som Pierre kendte, hen til ham, og han havde ikke tid til at besvare alle de spørgsmål om Moskva, der regnede ned over ham, eller lytte til alt, hvad man fortalte ham. Alle ansigter udtrykte livlighed og uro, men det forekom Pierre, at ophidselsen i nogle af disse ansigter hovedsagelig skyldtes spørgsmål om personlig succes; hans eget sind var optaget af det andet udtryk, han så på andre ansigter — et udtryk, der ikke handlede om personlige anliggender, men om livets og dødens universelle spørgsmål. Kutuzov lagde mærke til Pierres skikkelse og gruppen omkring ham.
»Kald ham herover,« sagde Kutuzov.
En adjutant meddelte Pierre Hans Durchlauchtigheds ønske, og Pierre gik hen mod Kutuzovs bænk. Men en militsmand nåede dertil før ham. Det var Dolokhov.
»Hvad laver den fyr her?« spurgte Pierre.

»Han er en type, der kryber ind overalt!« lød svaret. »Han er blevet degraderet, som De véd. Nu vil han kravle op igen. Han har foreslået en eller anden plan og har sneget sig ind i fjendens forpostlinje om natten.... Han er en modig fyr.«
Pierre tog hatten af og bøjede sig ærbødigt for Kutuzov.

»Jeg var klar over, at hvis jeg rapporterede til Deres Durchlauchtighed, ville De måske sende mig bort eller sige, at De allerede kendte det, jeg kom med, men så ville jeg ikke have tabt noget...« sagde Dolokhov.
»Ja, ja.«
»Men hvis jeg havde ret, ville jeg have ydet en tjeneste for mit fædreland, som jeg er rede til at dø for.«
»Ja, ja.«
»Og skulle Deres Durchlauchtighed have brug for en mand, der ikke skåner sit skind, så tænk venligst på mig.... Måske kan jeg vise mig nyttig for Deres Durchlauchtighed.«
»Ja... Ja...« gentog Kutuzov, og hans leende øje blev smallere og smallere, mens han betragtede Pierre.
Netop da trådte Boris med sin hofindsigt hen ved Pierres side nær Kutuzov og sagde i den mest naturlige tone, uden at hæve stemmen, til Pierre, som om han fortsatte en afbrudt samtale:
»Militsmændene har taget rene, hvide skjorter på for at være klar til at dø. Sikken heltemod, greve!«
Boris sagde tydeligvis dette til Pierre, for at Hans Durchlauchtighed skulle høre det, og det lykkedes.
»Hvad siger du om militsen?« spurgte han Boris.
»De forbereder sig på morgendagen, Deres Durchlauchtighed — på døden — de har taget rene skjorter på.«
»Ah... et vidunderligt, et mageløst folk!« sagde Kutuzov; og han lukkede øjnene og rystede på hovedet. »Et mageløst folk!« gentog han med et suk.
»Så De vil lugte krudt?« sagde han til Pierre. »Ja, det er en behagelig duft. Jeg har den ære at være en af Deres frues beundrere. Har hun det godt? Mit kvarter er til Deres tjeneste.«
Og som det ofte sker med gamle mennesker, begyndte Kutuzov at se sig åndsfraværende omkring, som om han havde glemt alt, hvad han ville sige eller gøre.
Så, tydeligvis idet han huskede, hvad han ville, vinkede han Andrej Kajsarov, sin adjutants bror, hen til sig.
»De vers... de vers af Marin... hvordan går de, hva'? Dem han skrev om Gerakov: 'Forelæsninger for korpset digtende'... Sig dem, sig dem!« sagde han, tydeligvis forberedt på at le.
Kajsarov fremsagde.... Kutuzov nikkede smilende i takt med versene.
Da Pierre havde forladt Kutuzov, kom Dolokhov hen til ham og tog hans hånd.

»Jeg er meget glad for at møde Dem her, greve,« sagde han højt, uden hensyn til de fremmedes tilstedeværelse og i en særlig beslutsom og højtidelig tone. »Aftenen før en dag, hvor Gud alene véd, hvem af os der overlever, er jeg glad for denne lejlighed til at sige Dem, at jeg beklager de misforståelser, der har været mellem os, og at jeg ikke ønsker, at De bærer nag til mig. Jeg beder Dem tilgive mig.«
Pierre så på Dolokhov med et smil, usikker på, hvad han skulle svare. Med tårer i øjnene omfavnede og kyssede Dolokhov Pierre.
Boris sagde et par ord til sin general, og grev Bennigsen vendte sig til Pierre og foreslog, at han skulle ride med ham langs linjen.
»Det vil interessere Dem,« sagde han.
»Ja, i høj grad,« svarede Pierre.
En halv time senere forlod Kutuzov stedet og tog til Tatarinova, og Bennigsen med sit følge, deriblandt Pierre, red ud langs linjen.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: Staggering amid the crush, Pierre looked around.
"Count Peter Kirilych! How did you get here?" said a voice.

Pierre looked round. Boris Drubetskoy, brushing his knees with his hand (he had probably dirtied them kneeling before the icon), came up to him smiling. Boris was elegantly dressed with a slightly military flair appropriate to a campaign. He wore a long coat and, like Kutuzov, had a whip slung across his shoulder.

Meanwhile Kutuzov had reached the village and seated himself in the shade of the nearest house, on a bench that one Cossack had run to fetch and another had hastily covered with a rug. An immense and brilliant suite surrounded him.
The icon was carried farther, accompanied by the crowd. Pierre stopped some thirty paces from Kutuzov, talking to Boris.
He explained his wish to be present at the battle and see the position.

"This is what you must do," said Boris. "I'll show you around the camp. You'll see everything best from where Count Bennigsen will be. I'm in attendance on him, you know; I'll mention it to him. But if you want to ride around the position, come with us. We're just going to the left flank. Then when we get back, please spend the night with me and we'll arrange a game of cards. Of course you know Dmitri Sergeevich? Those are his quarters," and he pointed to the third house in the village of Gorki.
"But I'd like to see the right flank. They say it's very strong," said Pierre. "I'd like to start from the Moskva River and ride around the whole position."
"Well, you can do that later, but the main thing is the left flank."
"Yes, yes. But where is Prince Bolkonsky's regiment? Can you show me?"
"Prince Andrew's? We'll pass it, and I'll take you to him."
"What about the left flank?" asked Pierre.

"To tell you the truth, between us, God only knows what shape our left flank is in," said Boris confidentially, lowering his voice. "It's not at all what Count Bennigsen intended. He meant to fortify that knoll quite differently, but..." Boris shrugged. "His Serene Highness wouldn't have it, or someone talked him out of it. You see..." But Boris didn't finish, because at that moment Kaisarov, Kutuzov's adjutant, came up to Pierre. "Ah, Kaisarov!" said Boris, addressing him with an easy smile. "I was just trying to explain our position to the count. It's amazing how his Serene Highness foresaw the French intentions!"
"You mean the left flank?" asked Kaisarov.
"Yes, exactly; the left flank is now extremely strong."

Though Kutuzov had dismissed all unnecessary people from the staff, Boris had managed to stay on at headquarters after the changes. He had attached himself to Count Bennigsen, who, like everyone Boris had ever attended, considered young Prince Drubetskoy an invaluable man.

In the higher command there were two sharply defined parties: Kutuzov's and Bennigsen's. Boris belonged to the latter, and while showing servile respect to Kutuzov, he skillfully created the impression that the old man wasn't up to much and that Bennigsen was running everything. Now the decisive moment of battle had come, when Kutuzov would either be discredited and power would pass to Bennigsen, or even if Kutuzov won, it would be felt that everything was Bennigsen's doing. In either case, many great rewards would be given for the next day's action, and new men would come to the fore. So Boris was full of nervous energy all day.

After Kaisarov, other people Pierre knew came up to him, and he hadn't time to answer all the questions about Moscow showered on him or to listen to everything they told him. All faces expressed excitement and apprehension, but it seemed to Pierre that the excitement in some of these faces was mainly about questions of personal advancement; his own mind, however, was occupied by the different expression he saw on other faces—an expression that spoke not of personal matters but of the universal questions of life and death. Kutuzov noticed Pierre's figure and the group gathered around him.
"Call him to me," said Kutuzov.
An aide told Pierre of his Serene Highness's wish, and Pierre went toward Kutuzov's bench. But a militiaman got there before him. It was Dolokhov.
"How did that fellow get here?" asked Pierre.

"He's a creature that worms his way in everywhere!" was the answer. "He was demoted, you know. Now he wants to claw his way back. He's been proposing some scheme or other and has crawled into the enemy's picket line at night... He's a brave fellow, though."
Pierre took off his hat and bowed respectfully to Kutuzov.
"I concluded that if I reported to your Serene Highness, you might send me away or say that you already knew what I was reporting, but then I wouldn't lose anything..." Dolokhov was saying.
"Yes, yes."
"But if I were right, I'd be rendering a service to my Fatherland, for which I'm ready to die."
"Yes, yes."
"And should your Serene Highness need a man who won't spare his skin, please think of me... Perhaps I may prove useful to your Serene Highness."
"Yes... yes..." Kutuzov repeated, his laughing eye narrowing more and more as he looked at Pierre.

Just then Boris, with his courtier's skill, stepped up to Pierre near Kutuzov and in the most natural manner, without raising his voice, said to Pierre as though continuing an interrupted conversation:
"The militia have put on clean white shirts to be ready to die. What heroism, Count!"
Boris clearly said this to Pierre intending to be overheard by his Serene Highness. He knew Kutuzov's attention would be caught by those words, and it was.
"What are you saying about the militia?" he asked Boris.
"Preparing for tomorrow, your Serene Highness—for death—they've put on clean shirts."
"Ah... a wonderful, a matchless people!" said Kutuzov; and he closed his eyes and swayed his head. "A matchless people!" he repeated with a sigh.
"So you want to smell gunpowder?" he said to Pierre. "Yes, it's a pleasant smell. I have the honor of being one of your wife's admirers. Is she well? My quarters are at your service."
And as often happens with old people, Kutuzov began looking around absent-mindedly, as if forgetting everything he wanted to say or do.
Then, evidently remembering what he wanted, he beckoned to Andrei Kaisarov, his adjutant's brother.
"Those verses... those verses of Marin's... how do they go? The ones he wrote about Gerakov: 'Lectures for the corps inditing'... Recite them!" said he, clearly preparing to laugh.
Kaisarov recited... Kutuzov nodded his head, smiling, to the rhythm of the verses.
When Pierre had left Kutuzov, Dolokhov came up to him and took his hand.

"I am very glad to meet you here, Count," he said aloud, regardless of strangers present, in a particularly resolute and solemn tone. "On the eve of a day when God alone knows who of us is destined to survive, I'm glad of this chance to tell you that I regret the misunderstandings between us and would wish you not to hold any ill feelings toward me. I beg you to forgive me."
Pierre looked at Dolokhov with a smile, not knowing what to say. With tears in his eyes, Dolokhov embraced Pierre and kissed him.
Boris said a few words to his general, and Count Bennigsen turned to Pierre and proposed that he ride with him along the line.
"It will interest you," he said.
"Yes, very much," replied Pierre.
Half an hour later Kutuzov left for Tatarinova, and Bennigsen and his suite, with Pierre among them, set out on their ride along the line.
